manifest.title: Discrete Probability: from sample spaces to conditional probability
manifest.author: L2T team
manifest.description: Canonical introductory probability methodology — coins, dice, bags, cards. Covers 10 concepts, 12 skills, 3 metaskills, 8 misconceptions. Primary statistical-testing domain for L2T simulation.

nodes.title: Sample space (Ω)
nodes.description: Set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. For one coin flip: {H, T}. For two dice: 36 ordered pairs.

nodes.title: Equally likely outcomes
nodes.description: Assumption (not a theorem) that each outcome of Ω has the same probability. Applies to fair coins/dice, not to weighted ones.

nodes.title: Event (A ⊆ Ω)
nodes.description: Subset of the sample space. 'At least one head in two flips' = {HH, HT, TH}.

nodes.title: Classical probability P(A)
nodes.description: P(A) = |A| / |Ω| when outcomes are equally likely. The most basic definition.

nodes.title: Complement rule
nodes.description: P(¬A) = 1 − P(A). Useful when 'not happening' is easier to count than 'happening'.

nodes.title: Independence
nodes.description: Two events are independent if knowing one doesn't change the probability of the other. Formally P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B).

nodes.title: Joint probability (independent)
nodes.description: For independent A, B: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B). Multiplication rule.

nodes.title: Mutually exclusive events
nodes.description: Two events that cannot both happen. P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B). Addition rule (special case).

nodes.title: Conditional probability P(A|B)
nodes.description: Probability of A given that B happened. P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B).

nodes.title: Expected value E[X]
nodes.description: Long-run average value of a random variable. E[X] = Σ x · P(X=x).

nodes.title: Addition rule for mutually exclusive events
Gambler's fallacy
nodes.description: After 5 heads in a row, tails is treated as 'more likely'. Independent events have no memory.

nodes.title: Equiprobability bias
nodes.description: Assuming all outcomes are equally likely without checking (e.g. sum=2 and sum=7 on two dice).

nodes.title: Conjunction fallacy
nodes.description: P(A∩B) > P(A) — impossible. Classic Linda-the-bank-teller setup.

nodes.title: Inverse confusion
nodes.description: Treating P(A|B) and P(B|A) as the same quantity.

nodes.title: Outcome approach
nodes.description: Predicting on a single outcome's probability ('I'll definitely win because P=1/6') instead of distribution thinking.

nodes.title: Addition without subtraction
nodes.description: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) when events are NOT mutually exclusive — missing the intersection term.

nodes.title: Assuming independence when there is none
nodes.description: Multiplying probabilities for dependent events such as drawing two cards without replacement.

nodes.title: Base rate neglect
nodes.description: Ignoring the prior probability in Bayes problems (medical-testing classics).

scaffolding_tasks.title: Two coins: at least one heads
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You flip a fair coin twice. What is the probability of getting at least one heads?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Fair die: even number
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die once. What is the probability of getting an even number?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Two dice: sum equals 7
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You roll two fair six-sided dice. What is the probability that their sum equals 7?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Bag of marbles: P(red)
scaffolding_tasks.statement: A bag contains 3 red marbles and 2 blue marbles. You draw one at random. What is the probability of drawing a red marble?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Standard deck: P(heart)
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You draw one card at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a heart?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Die: P(not 1)
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die once. Using the complement rule, what is the probability of NOT rolling a 1?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Two coins: P(not both tails)
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You flip a fair coin twice. What is the probability that NOT both flips are tails?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Three dice: P(at least one 6)
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You roll three fair six-sided dice. What is the probability of getting at least one 6? (Hint: complement of 'no 6 on any roll'.)

scaffolding_tasks.title: Counting face cards
scaffolding_tasks.statement: From a standard 52-card deck, how many cards are face cards (Jack, Queen, King)?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Counting in a committee
scaffolding_tasks.statement: A class of 30 students has 18 girls and 12 boys. The committee chair must be a girl. How many girls could be chosen?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Die: probability of 1 or 6
scaffolding_tasks.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die. What is the probability of rolling a 1 or a 6?

scaffolding_tasks.title: Small lottery: probability of winning
scaffolding_tasks.statement: A lottery sells 100 tickets, 5 of which are winners. You buy one ticket. What is the probability you win?

target_tasks.title: Two coins: P(HH)
target_tasks.statement: You flip a fair coin twice independently. What is the probability of getting heads on both flips?

target_tasks.title: Die-then-coin: P(6 AND H)
target_tasks.statement: You roll a fair die and then flip a fair coin. What is the probability of rolling a 6 AND flipping heads?

target_tasks.title: Two bags: P(red from both)
target_tasks.statement: Bag A has 4 red and 6 blue marbles; bag B has 3 red and 7 blue. You draw one marble from each bag independently. What is the probability that both are red?

target_tasks.title: Three coins: P(HHH)
target_tasks.statement: You flip a fair coin three times independently. What is the probability that all three flips show heads?

target_tasks.title: Die: P(roll 1 or 2)
target_tasks.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die once. What is the probability of rolling a 1 OR a 2?

target_tasks.title: Bag: P(red or blue)
target_tasks.statement: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue, and 5 green marbles. You draw one. What is the probability of drawing a red OR a blue marble?

target_tasks.title: Deck: P(ace or king)
target_tasks.statement: You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing an ace OR a king?

target_tasks.title: Deck: P(red or face card)
target_tasks.statement: You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a red card OR a face card (J, Q, K of any suit)?

target_tasks.title: Die: P(even or ≥4)
target_tasks.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die once. What is the probability of rolling an even number OR a number ≥ 4?

target_tasks.title: Two dice: P(first=1 or second=6)
target_tasks.statement: You roll two fair dice. What is the probability that the first die shows 1 OR the second die shows 6?

target_tasks.title: Deck: P(heart | red)
target_tasks.statement: You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck and are told it is red. What is the probability that it is a heart?

target_tasks.title: Die: P(6 | even)
target_tasks.statement: You roll a fair die and are told the result is even. What is the probability that the result is 6?

target_tasks.title: Two dice: P(sum=10 | first=4)
target_tasks.statement: You roll two fair dice. Given that the first die shows 4, what is the probability that the sum is 10?

target_tasks.title: Bag: P(second red | first red, no replacement)
target_tasks.statement: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. You draw two without replacement. Given the first is red, what is the probability the second is also red?

target_tasks.title: Medical test: P(disease | positive)
target_tasks.statement: A disease has prevalence 1%. A test has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Given a positive test, what is the probability the patient has the disease? (Approximate.)

target_tasks.title: Two coins: which one?
target_tasks.statement: Two coins look identical: one is fair, one always shows heads. You pick a coin uniformly at random and flip it once: it shows heads. What is the probability you picked the biased one?

target_tasks.title: Die payout: expected value
target_tasks.statement: A fair die is rolled. You receive in dollars the number rolled. What is the expected payout?

target_tasks.title: Independence: card draw then coin flip
target_tasks.statement: You draw a card from a deck (then return it), then flip a fair coin. Are the two outcomes independent events?
options: No — they share the same outcome space
Only if the card is red

target_tasks.title: Independence: replacement matters
target_tasks.statement: You draw two cards from a 52-card deck. Which scenario makes the two draws independent?
options: Neither — drawing cards is always dependent

target_tasks.title: Spam filter: P(spam | flagged)
target_tasks.statement: A spam filter flags 90% of true spam and 5% of legitimate emails. 30% of incoming emails are spam. If an email is flagged, what is the approximate probability it is actually spam?

target_tasks.title: Three coin flips: expected number of heads
target_tasks.statement: You flip a fair coin three times. What is the expected number of heads?

target_tasks.title: Lottery: expected payoff
target_tasks.statement: A lottery ticket: with probability 1/100 you win $1000, with probability 99/100 you win nothing. What is the expected payoff per ticket?

target_tasks.title: Coin observed frequency vs probability
target_tasks.statement: After 10 coin flips you observed 7 heads. What is the true theoretical probability of heads on the next flip (assuming the coin is fair)?

target_tasks.title: Small sample of die rolls
target_tasks.statement: You roll a fair six-sided die 5 times and observe a 6 twice. Does this prove the die is unfair?
options: Yes — the expected count is below 1
No — the sample is too small to conclude

target_tasks.title: Law of large numbers
target_tasks.statement: You flip a fair coin 1000 times vs 10 times and compute the observed frequency of heads. Which sequence is more likely to give a frequency closer to 0.5?

tasks.title: Light bulb works
tasks.statement: A box has 10 light bulbs, 3 of which are defective. You pick one at random. What is the probability it works?

tasks.title: Archery: target zone
tasks.statement: An archery target has 5 concentric zones of equal area. An arrow lands uniformly at random on the target. What is the probability it lands in the bullseye (innermost zone)?

tasks.title: Lottery: one winning number
tasks.statement: A lottery sells tickets numbered 1 through 1000. Exactly one number wins. You buy a single ticket. What is the probability you win?

tasks.title: Quality control: at least one defect
tasks.statement: A factory produces widgets, and each widget is independently defective with probability 0.02. You inspect a batch of 50. What is the probability that at least one is defective? (Approximate.)

tasks.title: Random password: at least one digit
tasks.statement: An 8-character password is generated by choosing each character independently and uniformly from {26 letters + 10 digits}. What is the probability it contains at least one digit?

tasks.title: Weather: rain in both cities
tasks.statement: On any given day, rain in city A occurs with probability 0.3 and rain in city B occurs with probability 0.4. Assume the two events are independent. What is the probability of rain in BOTH cities tomorrow?

tasks.title: Two machines: both fail
tasks.statement: Machine A fails with probability 0.05 on a given day; machine B fails with probability 0.08. Failures are independent. What is the probability both fail today?

tasks.title: Three emails: all spam
tasks.statement: Each incoming email is independently spam with probability 0.2. You receive three emails. What is the probability all three are spam?

tasks.title: Blood type: A or B
tasks.statement: In a large population, 42% have blood type O, 39% have A, 12% have B, and 7% have AB. A person is selected at random. What is the probability they have blood type A OR B?

tasks.title: Traffic light: red or yellow
tasks.statement: At any moment, the traffic light is red with probability 0.45, yellow with probability 0.05, and green with probability 0.50. You arrive at a random time. What is the probability the light is red OR yellow?

tasks.title: Survey: likes A or B
tasks.statement: In a survey of 100 people, 60 like product A, 50 like product B, and 30 like both. A person is selected at random. What is the probability they like A OR B?

tasks.title: Committee: member with skill X or Y
tasks.statement: A committee of 20 members has 12 who speak French, 8 who speak Spanish, and 4 who speak both. A member is selected at random. What is the probability they speak French OR Spanish?

tasks.title: Disease test: P(sick | positive)
tasks.statement: In a population, 5% have a certain disease. The test correctly identifies sick people 90% of the time and produces false positives in 10% of healthy people. Given a positive test result, what is the probability the patient is sick? (Approximate.)

tasks.title: Smoking: P(cancer | smoker)
tasks.statement: In a population, 20% are smokers and 80% are not. Among smokers 15% develop a particular cancer; among non-smokers 1% do. A person selected at random has the cancer. What is the probability they are a smoker? (Approximate.)

tasks.title: Factory: P(machine A | defect)
tasks.statement: Two machines produce widgets. Machine A makes 60% of widgets with a 2% defect rate; machine B makes 40% with a 5% defect rate. A randomly chosen widget is defective. What is the probability it came from machine A? (Approximate.)

tasks.title: Spam filter: P(spam | flagged)
tasks.statement: 20% of incoming emails are spam. A spam filter flags 95% of spam and 5% of legitimate emails. An email is flagged. What is the probability it is actually spam?

tasks.title: Courtroom: P(guilty | match)
tasks.statement: A DNA-style trace matches a suspect's profile. The probability of such a match if the suspect is guilty is 99%; if innocent, the prior 'random match' probability is 0.1%. Suppose the suspect was picked at random from a pool of 10000 and the prior probability of guilt is 1/10000. What is the posterior probability of guilt? (Approximate.)

tasks.title: Investment: expected payoff
tasks.statement: An investment pays off $1000 with probability 0.30, $500 with probability 0.50, and $0 with probability 0.20. What is the expected payoff?

micro_theories.title: What is a sample space?
micro_theories.content_markdown: A *sample space* (denoted Ω) is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. For a single coin flip, Ω = {H, T}. For rolling a fair die, Ω = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. For two coin flips in sequence, Ω = {HH, HT, TH, TT} — four outcomes. The key idea: outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive (every trial produces exactly one outcome from Ω).

micro_theories.title: When are outcomes equally likely?
micro_theories.content_markdown: Saying that outcomes are *equally likely* is an assumption about the experiment, not a theorem. A fair coin has P(H) = P(T) = 1/2 because we assume the coin is symmetric. A weighted coin with P(H) = 0.7 has the same sample space {H, T} but the outcomes are NOT equally likely. Always check the physical setup before assigning equal probabilities.

micro_theories.title: Events as subsets
micro_theories.content_markdown: An *event* is any subset of the sample space. If Ω = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, the event 'at least one head' is the subset {HH, HT, TH}. The event 'exactly two heads' is {HH}. Single outcomes are themselves events of size 1, and the entire Ω is the certain event.

micro_theories.title: Classical probability: favorable over total
micro_theories.content_markdown: When all outcomes in Ω are equally likely, P(A) = |A| / |Ω| — the count of outcomes in event A divided by the total count. For rolling a fair die, |Ω| = 6 and the event 'even' has |{2,4,6}| = 3, so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. This is the building block for everything that follows.

micro_theories.title: The complement rule
micro_theories.content_markdown: If A is an event, the *complement* ¬A is everything in Ω that is not in A. The complement rule says P(¬A) = 1 − P(A). This is often the fastest path to a probability: P(at least one 6 in 3 rolls) = 1 − P(no 6 in 3 rolls) = 1 − (5/6)³ ≈ 0.42.

micro_theories.title: Independence
micro_theories.content_markdown: Two events A and B are *independent* if knowing one does not change the probability of the other: P(A|B) = P(A). Physically, this often corresponds to separate trials with no interaction — two coin flips, two dice rolls, two unrelated machines. Drawing two cards *without replacement* is NOT independent: the first card changes the deck.

micro_theories.title: Multiplication rule for independent events
micro_theories.content_markdown: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) · P(B). So P(HH on two fair flips) = (1/2) · (1/2) = 1/4. The rule extends to more events: P(HHH) = (1/2)³ = 1/8. Always verify independence before multiplying — applying this rule to dependent events is a classical error.

micro_theories.title: Mutually exclusive events and the addition rule
micro_theories.content_markdown: Two events are *mutually exclusive* (or disjoint) if they cannot both happen in a single trial. Rolling a 1 and rolling a 2 are mutually exclusive — exactly one number comes up. For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can overlap, you must subtract the intersection: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B).

micro_theories.title: Conditional probability
micro_theories.content_markdown: Conditional probability P(A|B) reads 'the probability of A given that B happened'. By definition, P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B), provided P(B) > 0. This is how we update beliefs as we learn new information: given a positive test, what is the probability of disease? Conditioning typically *concentrates* probability on the part of Ω where B is true.

micro_theories.title: Expected value
micro_theories.content_markdown: The *expected value* E[X] of a discrete random variable is the weighted average of its possible values, weighted by their probabilities: E[X] = Σ x · P(X = x). It represents the long-run average over many independent trials, not a value you actually expect to see in any single trial. For a fair die paying its face value, E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5.
